Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Jason, a 39-year-old divorced construction worker, witnessed a traumatic event that profoundly altered his perception of himself and the world around him. It was a sunny summer day when he was working on a high-rise building in downtown Chicago. The project manager had assigned Jason to assist with securing scaffolding on the upper floors. As he was tightening bolts on the last level, he heard a loud crash and saw one of his coworkers fall from a higher floor, landing in an unmoving heap below. The event left an indelible mark on Jason's psyche. Whenever he thinks about it, vivid images flood his mind—pictures of his coworker falling through the air, the sound of metal clanging as the scaffolding gave way. The smell of sweat and dust that filled the construction site mixes with the acrid scent of smoke from the impact below, bringing back memories in a visceral manner. At times, Jason can even taste the grit of the concrete dust that he remembers swallowing during the chaos. Jason's coping mechanisms have evolved into maladaptive strategies over time. He has become adept at suppressing his anger, never allowing himself to feel or express it. When confronted with situations that could trigger an angry response, he simply shuts down and withdraws. This pattern has strained his relationships further since getting divorced; friends and colleagues often describe him as distant and unapproachable. In addition to suppressing his emotions, Jason frequently turns to gambling to distract himself from the overwhelming thoughts about the traumatic event. He frequents the local casino on weekends, betting large sums of money in an attempt to find a temporary sense of excitement or relief. This behavior has resulted in significant financial strain; he often finds himself short of rent and bills, which adds another layer of stress. Jason also engages in deliberate dissociation when confronted with intense memories. He tries to leave his body or blank out completely to avoid the distressing images that come flooding back. This escape mechanism allows him to temporarily detach from reality but has led to periods where he feels disconnected from everyday life and struggles to focus on work-related tasks. The trauma has shattered Jason's core beliefs about how the world operates. He now believes that his sense of security is completely destroyed, and he can no longer trust that bad things won’t happen again. This pervasive feeling of helplessness leaves him questioning his own abilities and adequacy as a worker and an individual. The thought of returning to the construction site where the traumatic event occurred fills him with dread. Over time, these symptoms have taken a toll on Jason’s work performance and personal life. He has become increasingly avoidant, often skipping meetings or delaying tasks that might remind him of the traumatic incident. His colleagues notice his withdrawal but are unsure how to help him. The financial strain from gambling has also created additional stressors, leading to further isolation. Despite these challenges, Jason finally decided to seek help after a particularly harrowing episode where he dissociated during a critical safety briefing at work. He was certain that if he continued down this path, his life would spiral out of control. Now, as he enters therapy, Jason is most afraid of the potential for more traumatic events and feels inadequate in dealing with them. However, he also holds onto hope that through therapy, he can find ways to reclaim a sense of safety and normalcy in his daily life. Jason’s journey towards healing begins with confronting these deeply rooted fears and maladaptive strategies while working on regaining control over his thoughts and actions. He is determined to rebuild his shattered beliefs and regain a sense of adequacy and security in the world around him.
